theory.intro: The **area** of a rectangle is the amount of surface it covers. Multiply its length by its width.
facts: Area is measured in square units: cm$^2$, m$^2$, km$^2$.
A square is a rectangle with equal sides, so its area is **side $\times$ side**.
To compare rectangles, calculate each area first. Rectangles with different dimensions can have the same area.
Use the same length unit. To find the number of tiles, calculate the area of the region and the area of one tile, then divide the region area by the tile area.
For paint or another covering, find the area first, then divide by the area covered by one litre or one piece.
steps: Read the length and the width (use the same unit for both).
Write the answer with squared units.

workedExamples.question_text: A rectangle is $7\text{ cm}$ long and $5\text{ cm}$ wide. Its length is increased by $2\text{ cm}$ while its width stays the same. Find the new area and how much the area increases.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Original area
$\begin{align*}A&=7\times5\\&=35\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
New length: $7+2=9\text{ cm}$.
New area
$\begin{align*}A&=9\times5\\&=45\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
$45-35=10\text{ cm}^{2}$
The area increases by $10\text{ cm}^{2}$.

workedExamples.question_text: A rectangular floor is $5.6\text{ m}$ long and $2.7\text{ m}$ wide. Rectangular tiles are $40\text{ cm}$ long and $30\text{ cm}$ wide. The tiles are placed with their lengths along the length of the floor. How many tiles are needed?
workedExamples.solution_text:
Use centimetres for all the lengths.
$5.6\text{ m}=560\text{ cm}$ and $2.7\text{ m}=270\text{ cm}$.
Area of the floor
$\begin{align*}A&=560\times270\\&=151200\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
Area of one tile
$\begin{align*}A&=40\times30\\&=1200\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
$151200\div1200=126$
$126$ tiles are needed.

workedExamples.question_text: A rectangular wall is $8\text{ m}$ long and $4.5\text{ m}$ high. One litre of paint covers $9\text{ m}^{2}$. How many litres are needed to paint the wall?
workedExamples.solution_text:
Area of the wall
$\begin{align*}A&=8\times4.5\\&=36\text{ m}^{2}\end{align*}$
$36\div9=4$
$4$ litres of paint are needed.

Rectangle A
$\begin{align*}A_{\text{A}}&=8\times3\\&=24\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
Square B
$\begin{align*}A_{\text{B}}&=5\times5\\&=25\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
$25-24=1\text{ cm}^{2}$
Square B has the larger area, by $1\text{ cm}^{2}$.

workedExamples.question_text: A rectangle measures $4\text{ cm}$ by $3\text{ cm}$. Both dimensions are doubled. Find the new area and state how many times as large it is as the original.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Original area
$\begin{align*}A_{\text{original}}&=4\times3\\&=12\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
New dimensions: $8\text{ cm}$ and $6\text{ cm}$.
New area
$\begin{align*}A_{\text{new}}&=8\times6\\&=48\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
$48\div12=4$
The new area is $48\text{ cm}^{2}$, which is $4$ times the original.

workedExamples.question_text: A rectangle measures $10\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$. Find its area. Compare the area increases when only the length increases by $2\text{ cm}$ and when only the width increases by $2\text{ cm}$. Which change gives the greater increase?
workedExamples.solution_text:
Original area
$\begin{align*}A&=10\times6\\&=60\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
Length increased by $2\text{ cm}$
$\begin{align*}A&=12\times6\\&=72\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
Increase: $72-60=12\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Width increased by $2\text{ cm}$ instead
$\begin{align*}A&=10\times8\\&=80\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
Increase: $80-60=20\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Increasing the width, the smaller dimension, gives the greater area increase.

mastery.question_text:
A rectangle measures $6\text{ cm}$ by $5\text{ cm}$.
Both the length and the width are doubled.
Find the area of the new rectangle in $\text{cm}^{2}$, and state how many times as large it is as the original.
mastery.solution_text:
$A_{\text{old}}=6\times5$
$=30\text{ cm}^{2}$
New dimensions: $12\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$.
$A_{\text{new}}=12\times10$
$=120\text{ cm}^{2}$
$120\div30=4$
The new area is $120\text{ cm}^{2}$, which is $4$ times the original.

mastery.question_text:
A rectangular courtyard is $12\text{ m}$ long and $7.5\text{ m}$ wide.
It is to be covered with rectangular pavers measuring $0.5\text{ m}$ by $0.3\text{ m}$.
How many pavers are needed?
mastery.solution_text:
Use metres for all the lengths.
Area of the courtyard
$A=12\times7.5$
$=90\text{ m}^{2}$
Area of one paver
$A=0.5\times0.3$
$=0.15\text{ m}^{2}$
$90\div0.15=600$
$600$ pavers are needed.

mastery.question_text:
A rectangle has length $12\text{ cm}$ and width $7\text{ cm}$.
Find its area.
If only the length increases by $3\text{ cm}$, by how much does the area increase?
If only the width increases by $3\text{ cm}$ instead, by how much does the area increase?
Which dimension gives the greater area increase?
mastery.solution_text:
Original area
$A=12\times7$
$=84\text{ cm}^{2}$
Length increased by $3\text{ cm}$
$A=15\times7$
$=105\text{ cm}^{2}$
Increase: $105-84=21\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Width increased by $3\text{ cm}$ instead
$A=12\times10$
$=120\text{ cm}^{2}$
Increase: $120-84=36\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Increasing the width, the smaller dimension, gives the greater area increase.
